editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: At that time, then, Pompey did these things; but in the following year, when Lucius Cotta and Lucius Torquatus were consuls, he made war both upon the Albanians and upon the Iberians. And he was forced to come into conflict with the latter first, and contrary to

In the following year Caesar wished to court the whole multitude, that he might attach them still more to himself. But wishing also to seem to do what pleased the men of power, that he might not have them as enemies, he often said to them that he would write nothing

Thus, then, were those campaigns brought to an end; but after this, when the winter had passed in which Cornelius Spinther and Metellus Nepos began their consulship, a third war arose for them. For the Belgae, dwelling along the Rhine in many and mixed

In Rome, then, these things happened, in the seven-hundredth year of its existence; but in Gaul Caesar, in the consulship of those same men, Lucius Domitius and Appius Claudius, among other things made ready ships midway between his own swift vessels and the merchantmen of the country, so that they might be as light as possible and at the same time hold out against the wave, and might not be damaged when standing on dry

At that time, then, he did these things; but afterward, having received a letter from Caesar to the senate, he came to Rome on the very first day on which Lentulus Cornelius and Claudius Gaius entered upon their office, and he did not hand it over to the consuls until they had assembled in the senate-house, lest they should take it somewhere outside and suppress it.

Such, then, was the battle; and from it Pompey at once despaired of all his fortunes, and no longer made any reckoning either of his own valour, or of the multitude of his remaining soldiers, or of the fact that fortune often in the briefest space restores those who have stumbled, although in the time before he had always, in all his reverses, kept the highest cheerfulness and the highest good hope.

At that time he did these things; but in the following year he was both dictator and consul, each for the third time, Lepidus serving with him in both offices. For after he had first been named dictator by him, he straightway sent him, on the completion of his praetorship, into the nearer Spain,

Caesar, then, was doing these things thus, as one who would also make an expedition against the Parthians; but a guilty frenzy fell upon certain men, through envy of his eminence and hatred of his having been preferred above them, and unlawfully killed him, gaining a new name of unholy renown, and scattered the things that had been voted,

Antonius, then, was doing these things; but Gaius Octavius Caepias (for so was named the son of Attia, Caesar's niece) was from Velitrae of the Volscians, and, being left an orphan by his father Octavius, was reared both by his mother and by her husband Lucius Philippus, and, growing up, lived with

When Cicero had spoken to this effect, Quintus Fufius Calenus rose and said: “In the ordinary course I should have had no need either to plead anything in Antony’s defence or to assail Cicero. Indeed I do not think it right in deliberations such as the present to do either, but simply to declare what one believes; for the one is the business of a law-court, the other of a council.

Having thus made their compact and sworn together, they hastened to Rome, in appearance as though all would rule on equal terms, but in mind as though each one of them would himself hold the whole power—though they had learned beforehand, most plainly even before and most clearly then, what was destined

Brutus, then, and Cassius thus perished, slain with the swords with which they had made away with Caesar; and the rest who had shared in the plot against him—some before, some then, some afterwards—were destroyed, save very few, as somehow justice required and the divine power led on, that they who had killed a man their benefactor, one who had advanced so far both in virtue and in fortune,

In the winter, then, in which Lucius Gellius and Cocceius Nerva were consuls, these things were so done; and Caesar, when the fleet had been made ready and spring set in, set out from Baiae and was conveyed along Italy, having no small hope of encompassing Sicily on every side. For he himself sailed with many ships, and Antony’s were already present at the strait; and Lepidus, though unwillingly,

The Roman people had been deprived of the democracy, yet had not been distinguished off into an exact monarchy; but Antony and Caesar still held affairs on equal terms, having divided up the greater part of them between themselves, and reckoning the rest in word common, but in deed appropriating it to themselves, as each of them was able somewhere to gain an advantage.

Such was the sea-battle they fought on the second of September. I have not mentioned the date without reason (for it is not my custom to do so), but because it was then for the first time that Caesar held the whole power alone,

These, then, were the deeds and the sufferings of the Romans under the kingship, under the republic, and under the dynasts, throughout seven hundred and twenty-five years. After this they began once more to be ruled, strictly speaking, by a single man, although Caesar had deliberated whether to lay down his arms and entrust affairs to the senate and the people.

These things took place at that time; and the next year Caesar held his sixth consulship, and did everything else according to the custom handed down from very ancient times, and delivered to Agrippa, his colleague, the bundles of rods in his turn, while he himself used the other set, and, when his term was complete, administered the oath

In the year following, in which Marcus Marcellus and Lucius Arruntius were consuls, the city was again flooded when the river overflowed, and many things were struck by thunderbolts, including the statues in the Pantheon, so that the spear even fell from the hand of Augustus. Distressed, then, both by the disease and by the

These things took place in the consulship of Iullus Antonius and Fabius Maximus; but in the following year Drusus was consul with Titus Crispinus, and to him there came signs that were not good; for many things, among others, were destroyed both by storm and by thunderbolts, and many temples too, so that even that of Capitoline Jupiter and those associated with him were damaged.

And indeed he framed a certain proposal concerning the land which he distributed to the whole crowd in such a way that not even a small part of it could be found fault with; and yet he made a pretence that he would not even introduce this, unless it were agreeable to them. So far as the law was concerned, then, no one could bring any charge against him; for the multitude of the

races, and reaching to the ocean over against Britain, had formerly some been at peace with the Romans and others taken no thought of them, but then, seeing Caesar prospering and fearing lest he set upon them too, they banded together, and using, except for the Remi, a common policy, both deliberated against the Romans and bound themselves by oath, putting Galba at their head.

For even so they held out a long while, being unwilling to read it aloud; but at last, under pressure from Quintus Cassius Longinus and Marcus Antonius, who were tribunes, they were compelled to make it public.

The cause was that in those former cases, being on the whole a match for his adversaries, he did not anticipate victory in his judgement, but, looking forward to the outcome of events on either side—while still confident and before coming to any consternation—he did not neglect to provide against the worse, and on this account he was neither compelled to give way to misfortunes and was easily able to renew the fight; but now, having hoped to surpass Caesar by far, he had made no provision beforehand.

But since this man has undertaken to abuse Antony out of the enmity that exists between them—a man whom, if he had done any wrong, he ought to have impeached—and has besides mentioned me with slander, as though he could not otherwise display his own cleverness unless he wantonly insulted somebody,

For to Lepidus a snake coiled about the sword of a centurion, and a wolf, entering the camp and his tent while he was at dinner and overturning the table, foreshadowed at once both his power and the trouble attending upon it; while to Antony milk that flowed round about the entrenchment, and a kind of singing that resounded through the night, foreshowed both his delights and

should suffer. And Caesar and Antony at once had the advantage over Lepidus, since he had not shared in their victory, and were destined before long to turn against one another also; for it is hard that three men, or even two, of equal honour, who have become masters of so great affairs out of war, should be of one mind.

had at any rate promised to come to his aid. And he was most confident in the height of his vessels and the thickness of their timbers; for they had been built exceedingly thick and exceedingly large, so as to carry the greatest possible number of marines (for they bore towers too, that they might fight as from a wall from a height) and themselves to withstand the rammings of the enemy, and to turn aside their rams, inasmuch as they made the collision the more violent.

But after this, when Sextus had perished and the Armenian had been taken, and the peoples who had made war on Caesar were quiet and the Parthian made no movement, then they openly turned against one another and the people was exactly enslaved. And these were the causes and pretexts of the war for them.

And in commemoration of it he dedicated to Apollo of Actium a trireme and a quadrireme, and the rest of the vessels in order up to one of ten banks of oars, taken from the captured ships; he built a larger temple, and instituted a quinquennial contest, sacred, with athletic and musical competitions and horse-racing (so they name the games that carry the privilege of public maintenance), naming it the Actia.

And the boy had just been born when Nigidius Figulus, a senator, straightway prophesied to him the

the destruction that would come of them. To these men, then, these things happened before they came into Italy; but to Caesar, just then, upon the compact, an eagle settled above his tent, and, when two ravens fell upon it and tried to pluck its feathers, killed them, thereby giving him the victory over both of them.

And on this account all that until then they had accomplished by agreeing for the overthrow of those who opposed them, this they now began to make the prizes of their rivalry with one another. For they at once redistributed the empire, and to Caesar fell Spain and Numidia, to Antony Gaul and Africa; and they agreed that, should Lepidus make any complaint at this,

With such reckonings Caesar hastened to Sicily. And as he was rounding the promontory called Palinurus, a great storm fell upon him; and this both destroyed many ships, and Menas, coming upon the rest while they were in confusion,

Antony charged Caesar that he had deposed Lepidus from his office, and had appropriated the territory and the force both of him and of Sextus, which ought to be common to them; and he demanded back the half of these, and of the soldiers whom Caesar had levied out of Italy, which belonged to

He also founded a city on the site of his camp, gathering some of the neighbouring peoples together and removing others to it, and gave it the name Nicopolis. The very ground on which he had pitched his tent he faced with square stones and adorned with the captured beaks of ships, setting up there an open-air shrine of Apollo.

both of them. In the present circumstances, then, he did everything else as was customary, and completed the census, and in it was styled Princeps of the senate, as had been the practice under the strict republic. He also completed and dedicated the temple of Apollo on the Palatine, with the precinct about it, and the libraries.

to appoint him dictator, and, shutting up the senate in the senate-house, compelled it to vote this, threatening to burn them, and afterwards, taking the twenty-four rods, approached him, begging him at once both to be named dictator and to become curator of the corn-supply, as Pompey once had been.

He promised to disband his legions and to lay down his command, provided Pompey should do the same; for so long as Pompey kept his arms, he said it was not just that he himself should be compelled to give up his own, lest he should be handed over to his enemies.

forced by those about him, he joined battle. And on this account, as soon as he was defeated, he was terribly dismayed and had neither any timely counsel nor any sure hope for renewing the hazard. For whenever anything befalls a man unexpectedly and with great unreason, it both humbles his spirit and confounds his reasoning, so that he becomes the worst and weakest judge of what must be

sole power; for he had best of all the men of his time discerned the ordering of the heavens and the differences of the stars, both what they bring to pass by themselves and what when they mingle with one another in their conjunctions and their separations, and on this account he incurred the charge, as it were, of carrying on certain secret

burned some and took others in tow. These things took place later. At the time he sent off a part of his fleet in pursuit of Antony and Cleopatra; and those ships did pursue them, but when the fugitives proved beyond catching, they turned back. With the rest of the fleet he took the enemy's entrenched camp, none opposing him because of their small numbers, and afterwards he overtook the remaining army on its way to Macedonia and brought it over without a battle.

at hand.' Now it is marvellous that such a voice should come to anyone from the divine power, yet I cannot disbelieve it; for it came to pass at once, since he turned back in haste and died on the road of a certain disease before reaching the Rhine.

Yet these men no longer warred against Caesar, but quietly both they and all the peoples that had previously sided with Rome came to terms,

At that time also an athletic contest was held, a wooden stadium having been built in the Campus Martius, and a gladiatorial combat took place with the captives.

No one voted that Pompey should give up his arms (for he held his forces in the suburbs), but all voted that Caesar should, except a certain Marcus Caelius and Curio, who

For these reasons, then, Pompey too, since he had foreseen none of them, was found both naked and defenceless—though perhaps, had anything been provided beforehand, he might without difficulty have recovered everything quickly. For many of those who had fought had survived, and he had other forces not small; and what is greatest, he had acquired much money and was master of all the sea, and the cities, both his own and those in Asia, loved him even in his misfortune.

For it is easier to find one good man than many;

And Augustus, learning beforehand that he was sick (for he was not far off), quickly sent Tiberius; and he found him still breathing, and on his death conveyed him to Rome, at first carrying him, as far as the winter quarters of the army, through the centurions and the tribunes, and from there through the foremost men of each city.

And he did both, as though intending to come to terms; but in fear, when he saw Pompey across, he fled to the Pelorus, which likewise flows in his realm; for the river which he might have prevented Pompey from crossing, this he himself drew on as he

should not please someone. But on the whole all the men of power who were outside the conspiracy were greatly displeased. And this very thing distressed them most, that he had so drawn up the measure that none could lay any charge against it, and yet it weighed heavily upon them all;

But at dawn, taking his cavalry and bidding the infantry follow, he overtook them, and when they stood to battle (for he was thought to be with the cavalry alone), he delayed until the infantry too came up, and so, surrounding them with his whole army, both cut down the greater part and brought over the survivors by agreement. And from this he won over some of the communities without a battle and others by war.

Contents. The following is contained in the thirty-ninth book of Dio's Roman History: 1. How Caesar made war upon the Belgae. 2. How Cicero returned from exile. 3. How Ptolemy, cast out of Egypt, came to Rome. 4. How Cato settled affairs in Cyprus. 5. How Pompey and Crassus were chosen consuls. 6. How the theatre of Pompey was dedicated. 7. How Decimus Brutus, Caesar's lieutenant, conquered the Veneti in a sea-fight. 8. How Publius Crassus, Caesar's lieutenant, made war on the Aquitani. 9. How Caesar, after warring with certain of the Celts, crossed the Rhine; and concerning the Rhine. 10. How Caesar crossed over into Britain; and concerning the island. 11. How Ptolemy was restored to Egypt by Gabinius, and how Gabinius was tried for it. The span of time is four years, in which the magistrates here numbered held office: Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther, son of Publius, and Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos, son of Quintus, consuls; Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus, son of Publius, and Lucius Marcius Philippus, son of Lucius, consuls; Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, son of Gnaeus, for the second time, and Marcus Licinius Crassus, son of Publius, for the second time, consuls; Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, son of Gnaeus, and Appius Claudius Pulcher, son of Appius, consuls.

For he thought that he would never have any power apart from them, and that he would never at any time give offence to either of them; nor again was he afraid lest, if they came to agreement, they should become stronger than himself; for he knew very well that he would prevail over the rest at once through their friendship, and over them themselves not long after through each other.

Pompey, then, since by doing nothing else he accomplished anything, turned openly to harshness, and from the open both said and did everything against Caesar. Yet he accomplished nothing.

And the proof is that he spared Sadalus the Thracian and Deiotarus the Galatian, although they had taken part in the battle, and Tarcondimotus, who held dominion over a certain part of Cilicia and had aided him very much toward his naval forces.

For many others fought for Caesar, and Lucius Paulus, the colleague of Marcellus, and Lucius Piso, his father-in-law, who was censor; for censors at this time were Appius Claudius and Piso, although against his will.

For why need one recount the others who sent their contingents, to whom likewise he granted pardon, taking from them only money? For he neither did them any other harm nor took anything away, although many had received many great things from Pompey, some long ago, some even then.

unholy toward his benefactor. With so great clemency and virtue did he, on the whole, treat all who had made war against him; indeed, the letters laid away that were found in Pompey's caskets—all that convicted certain men both of goodwill toward him and of ill-will toward himself—he neither read nor copied out, but

straightway burned them, that he might not be compelled to do anything dreadful on their account, so that for this too some hated those who had plotted against him. And this I have said not idly, but because Caepio Brutus Marcus, the man who afterward killed him, was both captured by him and saved.

arg. The following are contained in the forty-second book of Dio's Roman History: 1. How Pompey, defeated in Thessaly, fled to Egypt and died. 2. How Caesar, pursuing Pompey, came to Egypt. 3. How the affairs of Caesar and Pompey were reported at Rome, and what they voted to Caesar. 4. How those at Rome fell into sedition during Caesar's absence abroad. 5. How Caesar, making war on the Egyptians, subdued them and bestowed the kingdom upon Cleopatra. 6. How Caesar conquered Pharnaces. 7. How Caesar returned to Rome and ordered affairs there. 8. How Caesar made an expedition into Africa. Span of time: the remainder of the consulship of Gaius Julius Caesar (for the second time) and Publius Servilius Isauricus, and one other year, in which the magistrates here numbered were: Gaius Julius Caesar, son of Gaius, dictator for the second time; Marcus Antonius, son of Marcus, master of the horse; and as consuls, Quintus Fufius Calenus, son of Quintus, and Publius Vatinius, son of Publius.

At this same time also the wife of Pompey died after giving birth to a little daughter; and her body, whether the friends of Pompey and of Caesar so contrived, or some wishing otherwise to gratify them, men seized, as soon as she had received the eulogies in the Forum, and buried in the Campus Martius, although Domitius opposed it and said, among other things, that it was not lawful for her to be buried in the sacred place without some decree.

Marcellus, then, taking this up, and thinking that the senate would vote something dreadful both against Curio and, through him, against Caesar, put forward proposals

concerning him. Curio at first opposed any opinion being given concerning himself; but learning that the greater part of the senators then present some really favoured Caesar and others greatly feared him,

he permitted them to decide, only adding this much: "I am conscious to myself that I am doing the best and most advantageous things for my country; yet I deliver to you both my body and my soul, to use as you wish." Marcellus, then, having accused him as one who would assuredly be convicted, then, since

by the greater part he was acquitted, took it ill, and leaping out of the senate-house went to Pompey, who was in the suburb, and gave him, of his own accord, none having voted it, both the guarding of the city and two citizen-legions. And even then he would have failed of it, had not Servius Galba, who had campaigned with him, secretly and toward dawn, as praetor, given certain men the vote (although it was not permitted by the laws that any business be transacted before the people before the first hour). Contents. The following is contained in the fortieth book of Dio's Roman History: 1. How Caesar crossed over a second time into Britain. 2. How Caesar, on his return from Britain, again made war upon the Galatae. 3. How Crassus began to make war on the Parthians. 4. Concerning the Parthians. 5. How Crassus, being defeated by them, perished. 6. How Caesar subdued the whole of Transalpine Gaul. 7. How Milo, after killing Clodius, was condemned. 8. How Caesar and Pompey began to fall into discord. The span of time is the remainder of the consulship of Domitius and Appius Claudius and four other years, in which the magistrates here numbered held office: Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, son of Marcus, and Marcus Valerius Messalla, consuls; Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, son of Gnaeus, for the third time, and Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio, son of Nasica, consuls; Servius Sulpicius Rufus, son of Quintus, and Marcus Claudius Marcellus, son of Marcus, consuls; Lucius Aemilius Paulus, son of Marcus, and Gaius Claudius Marcellus, son of Gaius, consuls.

soldiers); but when they fell into discord, wishing both to take this back from him and besides to deprive him of yet another, he gave out that Bibulus needed soldiers against the Parthians, and that, in order that no new levies be made (for he said that the matter was urgent and that they had an abundance of legions), it was voted that each of them, himself and

Caesar, should send him one. And from this he sent none of those serving under him, but ordered that the army which he had given Caesar be demanded by those appointed for this purpose. And so in word both of them, but in truth Caesar alone, sent the
two; for he knew what was being done, but obeyed, not wishing to incur the charge of disobedience, especially as he intended on this pretext to enroll far more soldiers in their place.

These legions, then, were made ready as though to be sent against the Parthians, but when there was no need of them (for there was no use for them), Marcellus, earlier, fearing lest they be given back to Caesar, said that they ought to be in Italy, but then, as I said, handed them over to Pompey.

And since what was being done was at the close of the year, and was not likely to be in force long, inasmuch as it had seemed good neither to the senate nor to the people, he brought over to Pompey Cornelius Lentulus and Gaius Claudius, who were to be consuls the following year, and made them too give the same orders;

for since it was permitted even then to publish dispatches to those appointed to the offices and to do certain other things pertaining to their command even before it began, they thought themselves masters of this. And Pompey, although strict in everything else, nevertheless busied himself nothing, on account of his need of soldiers, either from whom or how he received them, but received them very gladly.

Yet nothing was done such as one would have expected to come from so great a daring, but, having only displayed their enmity toward Caesar, they themselves made ready nothing else strong, and gave him from this too a reasonable pretext for retaining the armies that were with him.
For Curio, on these grounds, made a long accusation before the multitude both against the consuls and against Pompey, and when he had completed his term of office, set out at once to Caesar.

arg. The following are contained in the forty-first book of Dio's Roman History: 1. How Caesar came into Italy, and how Pompey, abandoning it, sailed across to Macedonia. 2. How Caesar subdued Spain. 3. How Caesar sailed across to Macedonia against Pompey. 4. How Caesar and Pompey fought around Dyrrachium. 5. How Caesar conquered Pompey at Pharsalus. Span of time: two years, in which the magistrates here numbered were: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, son of Publius; Gaius Claudius Marcellus, son of Marcus, consuls. Gaius Julius Caesar, son of Gaius, for the second time; Publius Servilius Isauricus, son of Publius, consuls.
